summary:
The HYPER-SPEED study investigates the use of hyperspectral imaging during abdominal surgical procedures to identify various tissue types and to detect potential diseases or complications (e.g., post-surgery). This study is exploratory and observational, which means it analyzes data that are not part of the primary objectives of the study.

Hyperspectral imaging measurements are conducted in patients undergoing abdominal surgery with tissue removal, particularly in procedures involving the pancreas, liver, upper gastrointestinal tract, or colon. Study personnel establish contact with patients before the surgery.

On the day of surgery, in addition to documenting surgical details, hyperspectral images are captured. To unequivocally identify relevant anatomical structures, conventional photos of the surgical field are simultaneously taken, annotating the corresponding organs and vessels. This allows for subsequent allocation and analysis of the image material.

The exact timing of hyperspectral image acquisition depends on the type of procedure and the course of the surgery. In addition to images of the surgical field, pictures of removed tissue for histopathological examination are also taken.

After the surgery, relevant outcome parameters are collected on the day of discharge or 30 days after the surgery. This is done as part of routine examinations and visits that are part of the medical care of the patients. No additional measures are required for the patients, as existing data are used.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Planned surgery in one of the study-relevant areas of visceral surgery (Upper gastrointestinal tract: esophagus, stomach, duodenum, pancreas, liver and bile duct, small intestine, and colorectal procedures)
• Patient age ≥ 18 years
• Ability to independently provide written consent for study participation
Exclusion criteria:
- Emergency surgical procedure
• Pregnancy
• History of solid organ transplantation
• Presence of a septic condition at the time of the procedure
• Pre-existing medical conditions requiring intraoperative controlled hypotension
• Lack of capacity to provide informed consent
